summaries.example: Mia points at Sam and says, “He lives in Chicago.” Her thought is about Sam himself, not merely about “the person standing near the window.” If Sam and another person changed places, Mia would still be talking about Sam. This helps show the difference between thinking directly about someone and thinking about whoever fits a description.
summaries.summary: A proposition is what a sentence or thought says. A singular proposition is about a particular individual because that individual is a direct part of the proposition. “Sam is happy” might be a singular proposition about Sam. By contrast, “The tallest student is happy” may be about whoever fits a description, and “Some students are happy” is general. The article compares two large approaches. Fregeanism says that we think about objects through senses, or ways of presenting them. Russellianism says that at least some thoughts can contain the object itself. Several arguments support the Russellian idea. A pointing word like “he” can continue to be about the same person even when that person’s temporary features change. Words like “I” and “today” also seem to depend on the speaker and time, not only on a description in the speaker’s mind. A thought experiment with two matching regions of a world suggests that seeing and pointing at one person can make a thought about that person rather than about a similar twin. The article then explains problems. Objects can change, begin, or stop existing, while propositions are often treated as things that do not change. Philosophers therefore disagree about possible worlds, time, and how objects continue through change. The main lesson is that singular propositions may help explain reference and thought, but they create serious questions about possibility and time.
key_ideas: Some philosophers think thoughts about particular people or objects can include those very things. These are singular propositions.
Other philosophers think we reach every object through a description or a way of thinking about it.
Words such as “I,” “today,” and “here” depend on who speaks, when they speak, or where they are. This supports the idea that some thoughts are directly about individuals.
The article also asks difficult questions about change and possibility. If a person changes, or might never have existed, how can that person be part of an unchanging proposition?
The arguments support singular propositions, but they do not settle exactly which things we can think about directly.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic asks how words and thoughts connect with the world. It helps explain why “Mark Twain” and “Samuel Clemens” can give someone different information even though they name the same person, and why “I am tired” depends on who says it. It also connects language with bigger questions: What makes someone the same person over time? Could something have failed to exist? Understanding these questions teaches us how philosophers build arguments and compare competing explanations.

important_terms.definition: A proposition is what a sentence or thought says. It can be true or false, such as the claim that a mountain is tall.
A singular proposition is a proposition about one particular thing because that thing is part of the proposition itself.
A general proposition talks about things without focusing on one particular thing, such as “Some music is wonderful.”
A description identifies something by saying what features or job it has, such as “the person who invented bifocals.”
A demonstrative is a word or action, such as “this,” “that,” or pointing, used to pick something out in a situation.
A possible situation is a way things could have been, even if that situation is not the actual one.

questions_to_think_about: If you point to a red ball and say “This is mine,” are you talking about that ball itself or about something that fits a description?
Could two people know all the same facts about someone but still think about that person in different ways?
If a person moves from sitting to standing, what changes: the person, the thought, or the truth of the sentence?
Can you think directly about a place you have never visited?

summaries.example: At time t, Dana points to Paul on her right and says, “He lives in New Jersey.” A description such as “the person currently on Dana’s right” would refer to Charles instead if Paul and Charles switched places while keeping their other features. The original utterance still seems to concern Paul. Its truth would therefore remain stable in that counterfactual situation, while the descriptive claim would become false. This is the basic shape of the modal argument for direct reference.
summaries.summary: The entry investigates singular, or Russellian, propositions: structured propositions that are about an individual because that individual is a direct constituent. They contrast with general propositions and with particularized propositions, which concern an individual only through a condition that the individual satisfies. The issue sits at the intersection of semantics, philosophy of mind, and metaphysics. Fregean theories use senses or modes of presentation to explain why co-referring names can have different cognitive significance. Russellian theories instead allow direct thought of individuals, though Russell’s own acquaintance principle restricts which individuals can be constituents. Neo-Russellian views are often more permissive. Three arguments are examined. Kripke’s modal reasoning, adapted by Kaplan, contrasts a demonstrative utterance with descriptions based on contingent features. Indexical arguments from Kaplan and Perry emphasize that “I,” “today,” and “here” depend on context and that cognitive significance cannot simply be reduced to a descriptive sense. Strawson’s reduplication argument holds that, in a universe containing qualitatively matching regions, perception can make a thought determinately about one individual rather than its duplicate. These arguments support some form of direct reference, but they do not settle its scope. Singular propositions also create metaphysical difficulties. A proposition about an individual’s possible nonexistence seems to require the proposition to exist even where its constituent does not. A proposition about a past individual raises a parallel temporal problem. Further, if one individual changes from sitting to standing, philosophers must explain how one proposition can vary in truth across times without its object
key_ideas: The central dispute is whether propositions and thought contents can contain individuals themselves, or must contain senses, descriptions, or other intermediaries.
Frege’s puzzle about co-referring names motivates a distinction between reference and sense: a person may rationally accept one identity statement while rejecting another.

The modal argument says that a directly referring utterance can keep the same individual as its subject across counterfactual situations, unlike a description based on contingent features. Responses challenge the link between propositions and modal truth or replace contingent descriptions with rigidified properties.

Arguments from indexicals and demonstratives claim that cognitive significance cannot be identified with truth-conditional content alone. A person can use “today” or “I” competently without possessing a sufficient purely qualitative description.

The reduplication argument suggests that perceptual contact can fix which of two qualitatively similar individuals a thought concerns. It supports some direct reference but does not by itself determine how broad direct reference is.

Singular propositions generate modal and temporal problems. Philosophers respond using possibilism, actualism, eternalism, presentism, temporal parts, time-indexed properties, or other accounts of persistence and truth.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate clarifies several facts about language and thought that ordinary communication relies on: two names can present one person differently, demonstratives can pick out an individual in a context, and first-person beliefs can guide action even when a person lacks identifying information. Its metaphysical consequences are equally important. Any theory of singular propositions must say what propositions are made of, how they exist across possible worlds and times, and how changing objects can be constituents of apparently stable contents. The entry therefore shows how a question about a simple sentence can lead to disputes about identity, modality, time, and the structure of reality.

important_terms.definition: A proposition is a structured content that can be true or false, possess modal properties, and be believed, asserted, or otherwise taken as the object of an attitude.
A singular proposition is about an individual partly because that individual is a direct constituent of the proposition.
A general proposition does not concern any particular individual, while a particularized proposition concerns one indirectly through a condition or description.
Fregeanism explains reference and thought through senses, or modes of presentation, that are distinct from an expression’s reference.
Russellianism allows at least some thoughts to contain an individual directly rather than only a sense or description of it.
An indexical has a context-sensitive content; “I,” “here,” and “today” depend on features of an utterance or thought’s context.
A property that necessarily belongs to one individual and to no other is an individual essence; philosophers use such properties in responses to modal problems.
Perdurantism explains persistence through distinct temporal parts, while endurantism says one numerically identical object is wholly present at each time it exists.

questions_to_think_about: Does the fact that two names can be understood differently require different proposition contents, or could one proposition be grasped in different ways?
In the switching case, is the directly referring utterance true because it contains Paul, because it has a special semantic rule, or for another reason?
Can a person think about herself with “I” without having an accurate description of who she is?
If Socrates no longer exists, what could make the proposition “Socrates existed but does not exist” true?
Does an object that is sitting at one time and standing at another need temporal parts, time-indexed properties, or a different metaphysics of change?

summaries.example: Imagine Jordan points to Alex and says, “He is on the soccer team.” Now imagine a different possible situation in which Alex and Ben swap places, but Alex is still on the team and Ben is not. Jordan’s statement still seems true because it is about Alex. But “The person standing beside Jordan is on the team” would become false because Ben is now there. This supports the thought that pointing can connect a sentence directly with a person, rather than only with a description.
summaries.summary: The entry asks what propositions are and how they can be about particular individuals. A singular proposition is about an individual because that individual is a direct part of the proposition. This differs from a general claim, such as “Some songs are excellent,” and from a claim that reaches someone indirectly through a description, such as “The tallest student won.” Fregean philosophers explain thought using senses, or ways of presenting an object. This helps explain why “Mark Twain” and “Samuel Clemens” can lead to different beliefs even though they name the same person. Russellian philosophers allow at least some thoughts to include the individual directly. The entry considers three arguments for singular propositions. First, a modal argument compares a demonstrative sentence with descriptions whose identifying features could have been different. Second, arguments about indexicals and demonstratives say that words such as “I,” “today,” and “this” depend on context and cannot always be replaced by a purely descriptive thought. Third, the reduplication argument says that perceiving one person can make a thought about that person even when a similar person exists elsewhere. These arguments do not settle whether every person we think about is a direct constituent of thought. The article then examines problems. Propositions are often treated as stable abstract objects, but individuals can begin or stop existing and can change their qualities. Philosophers propose different answers involving possible worlds, presentism or eternalism about time, temporal parts, and time-related properties. The entry’s overall conclusion is balanced: singular propositions have strong motivation, but they also create deep questions about language, mind, time, and possibility.
key_ideas: Philosophers disagree about whether a thought about Alex contains Alex himself or contains a sense or description of Alex.
Fregean views emphasize that co-referring names can matter differently to a thinker. Russellian views emphasize that some thoughts can be directly about individuals.
The modal argument compares a pointing sentence with descriptions. A description can change its target when circumstances change, while the pointed-to person may remain the subject.
Indexicals create a special challenge. Someone can use “today” or “I” correctly without having a complete description of the day or person involved.
The reduplication argument imagines two regions with very similar people and surroundings. Seeing one person seems to make a thought about that person, not merely about whoever has certain qualities.
Singular propositions lead to questions about people who no longer exist, people who might never have existed, and people who change over time.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue matters because communication is not only about descriptions. When someone says “I,” “this,” or a person’s name, context and point of view can affect what is being thought about. The debate also explains why people can share information yet understand a statement differently. Finally, it links everyday examples of pointing and naming to large philosophical questions about what exists, how things remain the same, and what could have happened instead.

important_terms.definition: A proposition is the meaning or claim expressed by a sentence or thought. It can be true or false and can be believed or doubted.
A singular proposition is a claim about one particular person or thing because that individual is part of the claim itself.
A general proposition talks about a group without being about one chosen individual. A particularized proposition reaches an individual indirectly through a description.
A sense is a way an expression presents or describes something. Two names may have the same reference but different senses.
Direct reference is a way of picking out an individual without doing so merely through a description of that individual’s properties.
An indexical is a word whose content depends on context, such as “I,” “here,” or “today.”
A counterfactual situation is a way the world could have been, used to test whether a claim would remain true under different conditions.
A temporal part is a time-limited part of an object, such as an object during one moment, proposed by some theories of change.

questions_to_think_about: If “Clark Kent” and “Superman” refer to the same person, why might someone accept one sentence and reject the other?
When you say “I am hungry,” must you know facts about your name, history, or location?
Would pointing still identify one person if an identical-looking duplicate stood far away?
How should a theory explain a true statement about someone who lived long ago?
When a person changes from sitting to standing, is the person the same, or are there different time-slices of that person?
